title: Recursion
tagline: A function that calls itself — elegant, dangerous, and essential for trees, graphs, and divide-and-conquer algorithms.

sections.content:
**Recursion** is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. It sounds circular, but the key is that each call works on a *simpler* input until it reaches a case trivial enough to answer directly — the **base case**. Without the base case, recursion is just an infinite loop that crashes the stack.

Recursion shows up everywhere in CS: traversing trees and graphs, parsing nested structures, implementing divide-and-conquer algorithms (merge sort, quicksort), and writing compilers. Understanding *why* it works — and why it can explode — requires a clear mental model of the call stack.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Call factorial(4)"] --> B["factorial(4)\n= 4 * factorial(3)"]
  B --> C["factorial(3)\n= 3 * factorial(2)"]
  C --> D["factorial(2)\n= 2 * factorial(1)"]
  D --> E["factorial(1)\nbase case: return 1"]
  E -->|"unwind"| D2["2 * 1 = 2"]
  D2 -->|"unwind"| C2["3 * 2 = 6"]
  C2 -->|"unwind"| B2["4 * 6 = 24"]
  B2 --> F["Result: 24"]
sections.caption: Each recursive call pushes a new stack frame. The base case stops the descent; return values propagate back up as frames are popped.

sections.title: Russian Nesting Dolls
sections.content:
Imagine a set of Matryoshka (Russian nesting) dolls. To find the smallest doll inside, you open the outermost one and look inside. If there is another doll, you open that too — and keep going. Eventually you reach a doll with *nothing* inside — the **base case**. You report 'found the smallest one!' and hand that information back through every outer doll you opened.

Each 'opening' is a recursive call. Each 'handing back' is a return. The stack is the physical pile of open doll halves on the table — the deeper you go, the bigger the pile. If the dolls were infinitely nested, the pile would topple — that is a **stack overflow**.

Every recursive function has exactly two parts. The **base case** is the condition that stops recursion and returns a concrete result without another call. The **recursive case** calls the function with a simpler argument, trusting that call to eventually resolve. If either part is wrong — base case never triggered, or the recursive case does not shrink the problem — you get infinite recursion and a stack overflow.

Each call creates a new **stack frame** with its own local variables. When `factorial(4)` calls `factorial(3)`, frame 4 is paused on the stack while frame 3 runs on top. When frame 3 returns, frame 4 resumes. Frames accumulate like a tower during descent and collapse during unwind. For input of size *n* that is *n* frames simultaneously — O(n) space from the call stack alone.

**Recursion vs. iteration:** any recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively (with an explicit stack if needed), and vice versa. Iteration is usually faster because it avoids frame push/pop overhead. Recursion is cleaner for inherently hierarchical problems — tree traversals, combinatorial search, parsing. A related idea is **tail-call optimization (TCO)**: when the recursive call is the very *last* operation (a tail call), a smart runtime can reuse the same frame, giving O(1) stack space. V8 (Node.js / Chrome) does not implement TCO despite it being in the ES2015 spec — in practice JavaScript recursion always grows the stack.

sections.caption: Stack grows right during descent (each call pushes a frame) and shrinks left during unwind (each return pops a frame).

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Factorial is the classic pattern: one base case, one shrinking recursive call. Naive Fibonacci calls itself twice per call, producing O(2^n) total calls — disastrously slow for large n. Adding a `memo` object (line 15) caches each result and reduces time to O(n). Tree traversal (line 24) shows why recursion excels at hierarchical data: the code maps naturally onto the structure, with each subtree handled by an identical sub-problem.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Before writing any recursive function, answer two questions:** (1) What is my base case — and is it definitely reachable from every possible input? (2) Is my recursive call truly working on a *smaller* sub-problem? If both are yes, the function terminates. If either is no, you have an infinite loop waiting to happen.

items: Every recursive function needs a **base case** (returns directly) and a **recursive case** (calls itself with a strictly smaller input).
Each call pushes a new **stack frame**; recursion of depth n uses O(n) stack space — very deep recursion causes a stack overflow.
Naive recursion can be exponentially slow (e.g., Fibonacci O(2^n)); **memoization** caches sub-results and reduces time to O(n).
Recursion is cleaner for hierarchical problems (trees, graphs, parsing); iteration is faster because it avoids frame push/pop overhead.
**Tail-call optimization** could reuse stack frames for tail-recursive calls, but V8 does not implement it — in JavaScript, all recursion grows the stack.

quiz.question: What is the base case in a recursive function?
options: The call that makes the function run faster
The condition that stops recursion and returns a direct result
The first call to the function from outside
The part that calls the function with a larger argument
quiz.explanation: The base case is the termination condition. It returns a concrete answer without making another recursive call. Without it recursion is infinite.

quiz.question: What happens to the call stack as a recursive function descends deeper?
options: Old frames are reused, so stack size stays constant
A new frame is pushed for each call, growing the stack
The stack is cleared before each recursive call
Frames are stored on the heap instead
quiz.explanation: Each recursive call pushes a new stack frame with that call's local variables and return address. Stack size grows proportionally to recursion depth.

quiz.question: What is the value of `factorial(4)` where factorial(n) = n * factorial(n-1) and factorial(1) = 1?
quiz.explanation: factorial(4) = 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 24. The call unwinds: factorial(1)=1, factorial(2)=2, factorial(3)=6, factorial(4)=24.

quiz.question: What causes 'RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded' in a recursive function?
options: The function returns a value that is too large
The base case is never reached, so frames accumulate until the stack overflows
The recursive case uses too much heap memory
The function is called from global scope
quiz.explanation: When the base case is missing or unreachable, the function keeps calling itself and pushing frames until the stack's size limit is exceeded.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of the naive recursive Fibonacci `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: Each call fans out into two more calls, forming a binary tree of calls. The total number of calls roughly doubles for each increment of n, giving O(2^n).

quiz.question: How does memoization improve naive recursive Fibonacci?
options: It converts recursion to iteration automatically
It caches results of sub-problems so each is computed only once
It increases stack size to avoid overflow
It sorts the recursive calls for efficiency
quiz.explanation: Memoization stores the result of each fib(k) the first time. Subsequent calls for the same k return the cached value in O(1), reducing overall time to O(n).

quiz.question: What is the space complexity (call-stack depth) of a recursive function that calls itself n times before the base case?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
quiz.explanation: At maximum depth all n frames are on the stack simultaneously, giving O(n) space complexity from the call stack alone.

quiz.question: What is a tail call?
options: The first call to a recursive function
A recursive call where the call is the very last operation before returning
A call that terminates recursion
A call made from inside a loop
quiz.explanation: A tail call occurs when the recursive call is the absolute last thing the function does — its return value is immediately returned with no further computation.

quiz.question: Does V8 (Node.js / Chrome) support tail-call optimization (TCO)?
options: Yes — tail-recursive functions use O(1) stack space
No — V8 does not implement TCO; tail calls still grow the stack
Yes, but only in strict mode
Only for async functions
quiz.explanation: TCO is in the ES2015 spec but V8 deliberately does not implement it. In Node.js, tail-recursive calls still push new frames, so stack usage is O(n) regardless of call structure.

quiz.question: Which problem is recursion LEAST suitable for compared to iteration?
options: Traversing all nodes in a binary tree
Parsing a nested JSON structure
Summing a flat array of one million numbers
Implementing merge sort
quiz.explanation: Summing a flat list iteratively uses O(1) stack space and is straightforward. Recursing over one million elements risks a stack overflow and adds frame overhead unnecessarily.
